Faculty Spotlight
Nirmal Ghimire
Scientists at the University of Notre Dame synthesized a material that exhibits a rare and promising form of magnetism known as altermagnetism, which could reshape how computers store and process information in the future, a new study in Nature Communications shows.
Scientists have long sought out new methods that can support the future of ultra-fast and energy efficient electronics, said Nirmal Ghimire, associate professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy. Ghimire and collaborators synthesized single crystals of a compound called called CoNb₄Se₈ that exhibits altermagnetism, according to the study.
“This is a brand-new type of magnetism, realized just within the last few years,” said Ghimire, who is affiliated with Notre Dame’s Stavropoulos Center for Complex Quantum Matter.

Faculty Spotlight
Yi-Ting Hsu
Can a superconductor turn heat flow into a detectable electrical signal without the motion of magnetic vortices? This response, known as the Nernst effect, was long thought to be hidden because superconductors carry current without a voltage drop and screen the resulting electrical current. A recent study led by Postdoctoral Research Associate Tzu-Chi Hsieh and Professor Yi-Ting Hsu in the Department of Physics and Astronomy at the University of Notre Dame sheds new light on this problem and was selected as an Editors’ Suggestion in Physical Review Letters.

Faculty Spotlight
Dafei Jin
Dafei Jin, associate professor in the Department of Physics and Astronomy in the College of Science at the University of Notre Dame, is one of 21 researchers who received grants from the 2026 Gordon and Betty Moore Foundation’s Experimental Physics Investigators Initiative.
Jin will join experimental physicists from the previous four cohorts in advancing the frontiers of fundamental research, according to the foundation.
Full story here.
Faculty Spotlight
Kevin Lannon
University of Notre Dame physics professor Kevin Lannon in the Department of Physics and Astronomy has received the Meenakshi Narain Mentoring Award from the American Physical Society (APS), an honor that celebrates his commitment to his student advising and leadership within the field of particle physics.
Full story here.
Faculty Spotlight
Nirupama Sensharma
Nuclear power, to many people, is a daunting field surrounded by stigmas and misconceptions. To Assistant Professor Nirupama Sensharma, however, nuclear energy presents an incredible opportunity for scientific growth.
Sensharma joined the faculty in the Department of Physics & Astronomy in August 2026. Her research centers on how the atomic nucleus behaves under different conditions, identifying deformations in nuclear shapes and analyzing their behavior. Beyond the laboratory, Sensharma is passionate about educating the public on the benefits of nuclear science.
